strengths: Addresses a practical and important problem (real-time streaming infinite-length avatar generation) with strong experimental validation across multiple benchmarks and metrics
Comprehensive technical framework thoughtfully combining multiple mechanisms (TPP, RSFM, History Corrupt, AAS) to solve interconnected challenges of latency and long-horizon consistency
Strong empirical results with competitive or superior performance on GenBench and AVSpeech, validated by extensive ablations (Tables 3-4, 7) and user study confirming perceptual alignment
Achieves practical 20 FPS streaming performance on 5 H800 GPUs with detailed runtime analysis and efficiency characterization
Extensive supplementary material with algorithms, extended experiments to 10,000 seconds, cross-dataset validation, and architectural justification
Well-motivated design choices (block-wise causal masking, rolling sink frame mechanism, adaptive attention sink) specifically tailored to streaming avatar generation
weaknesses: Limited fundamental algorithmic novelty - primarily combines existing techniques (diffusion models, SFDM from prior work, temporal adaptation) rather than introducing new algorithms or theory
Incomplete baseline comparisons missing direct evaluation against StreamDiff and LongLive; limited methods in AVSpeech benchmark; no computational cost comparison with baselines
Significant domain gap in evaluation - training only on 5-second clips with inference extrapolating to 10,000+ seconds (200× extrapolation) lacks rigorous justification of generalization capability

Technical clarity issues including sparse explanation of block-wise noise scheduling, incomplete specification of training convergence criteria, and important insights (History Corrupt effectiveness) relegated to appendix
User study limited in scope (20 participants, 30 videos) for supporting claims about human perception; custom OOD evaluation limited to GenBench dataset without external validation
Reproducibility concerns including unspecified hyperparameters (loss weights, learning rates per training stage), unavailable code, and challenging dataset acquisition
High computational requirements (5 H800 GPUs for 20 FPS) with no analysis of scaling properties; TPP framework complexity may limit adoption
Evaluation metrics including custom Sync-C/Sync-D lack detailed methodology in main text and comparison with standard audio-visual synchronization metrics from literature

strengths: Achieves first practical real-time streaming of 14B diffusion model for infinite-length avatar generation at 45 FPS with 1.21s TTFF on 5 H800 GPUs - a significant engineering accomplishment

Well-designed system combining complementary technical strategies: two-stage training (diffusion forcing + self-forcing), three long-horizon stability mechanisms (History Corrupt, Adaptive Attention Sink, Rolling RoPE), and system-level Timestep-forcing Pipeline Parallelism

Comprehensive experimental validation with extensive ablations (Tables 3-6), long-horizon evaluation to 10,000+ seconds, multiple metrics (ASE, IQA, audio-visual sync, identity consistency), user study with perceptual evaluation, and comparisons against 6 state-of-the-art baselines
Introduces GenBench benchmark for long-form avatar video evaluation exceeding 5 minutes, enabling reproducible evaluation and supporting future research

Solid technical soundness with proper justification of design choices through ablations, detailed pseudocode for reproducibility (Algorithms 1-4), and commitment to release code and evaluation scripts
Clear presentation with effective technical diagrams explaining architecture (Figs. 2, 9-10) and inference procedures, making complex system design accessible
Addresses ethical considerations including privacy, consent, and responsible deployment guidelines for audio-driven avatar generation
weaknesses: Limited fundamental algorithmic novelty - individual components (History Corrupt heuristic, Adaptive Attention Sink adaptation, Rolling RoPE modification, TPP parallelization) are incremental adaptations of known techniques; novelty primarily in system combination rather than novel algorithms

Training-test distribution mismatch: model trained on 5-second clips but evaluated at 10,000 seconds; while impressive, this extrapolation beyond training distribution deserves deeper analysis of why stable generation persists

Evaluation specialized to talking-head scenarios on GenBench; generalization to diverse avatar types (full-body, stylized, non-human characters) and other domains not explored, limiting generalizability claims

Incomplete technical justifications: History Corrupt pattern choice lacks ablation, RoPE offset range (~40k) not principled, why three distinct strategies are necessary insufficiently explained beyond empirical evidence

Scalability concerns: evaluation uses single 14B architecture; generalization to different model sizes/architectures unclear; single-GPU throughput substantially lower, limiting practical accessibility despite claiming real-time capability
Hardware dependency: requires 5 H800 GPUs for 45 FPS; cloud deployment costs and single-GPU performance implications not discussed; limits reproducibility and practical deployment

Overstated claims about 'infinite length' despite practical limits under specific conditions (static-scene priors, training on 5s clips); interaction latency requirements for bidirectional telepresence not discussed
Missing efficiency analysis: no energy consumption, carbon footprint, or cost comparison for cloud deployment; memory requirements and scalability with fewer GPUs not thoroughly explored

Audio conditioning limited to English-centric dataset (AVSpeech); sensitivity to audio quality/encoding and cross-language generalization not explored despite audio being central to driving avatar motion

Metric limitations: audio-visual synchronization metrics (Sync-C/D) rely on pre-trained models that may not perfectly capture human perception; broader perceptual evaluation beyond user study would strengthen claims

strengths: Tackles a genuinely challenging and practically important problem combining streaming, real-time inference, and infinite-length generation at 14B scale
Comprehensive two-stage training framework with well-motivated complementary strategies (History Corrupt, AAS, Rolling RoPE) addressing specific failure modes
Impressive empirical results: 45 FPS with 1.21s TTFF, outperforms baselines across multiple metrics, maintains quality at 10,000+ seconds—unprecedented for diffusion avatars
Thorough experimental rigor with extensive ablations (Tables 3-6), user study with 20 participants, and reproducibility details enabling community validation
TPP (Timestep-forcing Pipeline Parallelism) is a creative engineering contribution solving sequential bottlenecks in diffusion sampling
GenBench benchmark with diverse characters and long-duration videos will benefit future research; clear commitment to release data and code
Includes ethical considerations for responsible deployment of avatar generation systems
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: History Corrupt, AAS, and Rolling RoPE are incremental optimizations; Self-Forcing and DMD are existing techniques—contributions are primarily engineering-focused rather than introducing fundamentally new algorithms or theory

Overstated 'Infinite Length' claim: Table 7 shows measurable quality drift over 10,000 seconds (Dino-S 0.96→0.95); extrapolation is bound by RoPE positional divergence and 5-second motion-frame context window

Incomplete baseline comparisons: Missing direct comparison with LongLive [50] (also addresses long-form streaming); most baselines use smaller models; WanS2V (2025) is very recent; no cross-domain or few-GPU scaling studies

Lack of theoretical justification for long-horizon capability: Why these specific strategies enable extrapolation is not analyzed; KV cache noise scheduling appears ad-hoc without principled design justification

Narrow scope and generalization concerns: Evaluated only on talking-head avatars from AVSpeech; no cross-domain experiments or evaluation on different avatar types—avatar-specific design choices may not transfer

High computational cost limits deployment: Requires 8 H800 GPUs; end-to-end latency including network transmission for actual streaming scenarios not analyzed; TTFF of 1.21s may not meet interactive requirements

Audio-visual synchronization analysis: Sync metrics depend on ground-truth videos; validity unclear for extreme extrapolation; limited study of failure modes at 10,000+ seconds; minor flicker (T.Flicker 0.97) suggests some instability
Limited justification for design choices: Why 5-second motion frames are optimal, why specific noise schedules work best (Table 6), why block size 3 is default (Table 10 shows marginal differences)
